name: Babylonian legal judgments on Hammurabi’s stela
description: A Babylonian royal monument sets out case-form legal provisions concerning family, property, work and trade.

impact.note: One monument, not the first law collection, whose text scribes of one civilisation copied for centuries and which shaped a few later collections.

date.label: Hammurabi’s reign, approximately 1792–1750 BCE
date.basis: The museum or heritage description provides an approximate period, not an exact year.

events.statement: A stone monument bearing Babylonian legal judgments was inscribed during Hammurabi’s reign.

evidence.supports: Dates the inscribed stela to around 1750 BCE and describes 282 judgments on family, property, commerce and labour; cautions against treating it as a modern code.
Catalogues the inscription as Old Babylonian and dates it to Hammurabi’s reign, 1792–1750 BCE, with creation in Mesopotamia.
Scholars divide the text into 282 paragraphs, but part of the stela was erased and its contents were partly reconstructed from duplicate tablets.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest event established in the sources collected here; not a claim of global priority.

caveats: A surviving royal text is evidence of legal claims and categories, not proof that every judgment was enforced. Earlier legal traditions existed; the Louvre cautions that this was not a modern comprehensive code. The monument was later removed to Susa. Westbrook describes part of the stela as erased and partly reconstructed from other tablets; the conventional numbering of 282 does not mean that 282 provisions remain intact on this monument. The case-form text does not itself prove each provision records an actual court decision.

research.note: Independent reader checked the dated event, stated scope and event-specific contributions against the cited passages; other facets retain their stated basis. The Louvre count is qualified by Westbrook’s discussion of erased columns and scholarly reconstruction.

measures.subject: Modern scholarly division of Hammurabi’s legal collection
measures.conditions: Louvre reports 282 judgments; Westbrook describes 282 scholarly numbered paragraphs, including erased material partly reconstructed from other tablets. Not 282 intact judgments readable on the surviving stela.
